items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘For Panama, it is life or death’: how drought is choking the canal that feeds a nation
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Failed rains and a dire El Niño threaten the waterway that sustains the country, with farmers selling cattle to survive

The cattle should be ambling, grazing contentedly, through Robert Delgado’s fields. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze.

In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Stefan Sagmeister’s new shoe designs are actually walking infographics
items.content_html:
Data visualization turns charts, data, and statistics into something easier to comprehend. Turning that data viz into shoes makes the data into a functional conversation starter.

That’s what the Austrian graphic designer Stefan Sagmeister did with two shoes he designed for Ekn, a German footwear brand, that are on view at his exhibition Finally, Something Good at the Paris gallery Gaîté Lyrique through April 2027.

Sagmeister says the exhibition is meant to look at the world over the long term rather than through daily news. Each shoe uses data to tell a story: one about renewable energy, and the other about homelessness. The key to understanding what the shoes say is written in the footbed.

The Bring It On, a multicolored sneaker about renewable electricity, uses data from the Energy Institute’s 2024 Statistical Review of World Energy to inform the relative sizes of color panels on its sides, with each leather panel representing a different energy source. Yellow, the largest color, represents hydropower, followed by black for wind, pink for solar, and red for all other renewables.

“Wonderfully, the shoe is already out of date,” Sagmeister tells Fast Company. “In the 2025 figures, published this summer, solar passed wind for the first time, so today the pink panel should be slightly bigger than the black one.”

His other shoe, Like a Complete Unknown, is a boot that uses circles to represent the relative homeless populations of six countries. The area of each circular appliqué corresponds to the number of people who are living in the streets and public spaces per 100,000 inhabitants, according to OECD data. The biggest circles are for the U.S., at 76, and Germany, at 46, followed by the U.K. (16), France (8), Mexico (5), and Japan (2).

“Countries count differently, so the numbers are not perfect, but Mexico, a much poorer country, reports a fifteenth of the American rate, and a gap that size is not only a counting difference,” he says. Sagmeister volunteered for the Coalition for the Homeless, an advocacy and service organization, and says what stayed with him from that experience was why some countries handle the same problem so much better than others.

The shoes are available for purchase on Ekn’s website. Both retail for more than $300, of which 10% goes either to the climate innovation think tank Future Cleantech Architects or the Coalition for the Homeless in New York, respectively. Sagmeister sees the inherent awkwardness between homelessness data and a boot costing 350 Euros, and says a donation “doesn’t make that go away.” He hopes people will take away that neither the data behind renewable energy nor homelessness is fate.

“When the number of people sleeping in the street runs from two to 76 per 100,000 across six countries,” he says, that shows “it’s about decisions, and decisions can be made differently.”

items.title: [MacRumors] GM Says Apple Wallet Car Keys Coming to These Vehicles
items.content_html:
In a late September press release that we just discovered now, GM announced that it has started rolling out Apple Wallet car key support in select Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC vehicle models, with additional models to follow over time.


Google Wallet and Samsung Wallet will also be supported, with a related Samsung press release mentioning availability in the U.S. and Canada.

GM said the rollout will occur as follows, with model years listed in parentheses.

September–October 2026



  • Cadillac Vistiq (2027)

  • Cadillac Optiq (2026–2027)

  • Cadillac Lyriq (2025–2027)



December 2026



  • Cadillac Escalade (2027)

  • Cadillac Escalade IQ/IQL (2027)

  • Chevrolet Suburban (2026–2027)

  • Chevrolet Tahoe (2026–2027)

  • GMC Yukon (2026–2027)

  • GMC Yukon XL (2026–2027)

GM said customers will see a notification in the "What's New" section of their vehicle's mobile app when digital key support is available.

Apple Wallet's car key feature allows you to use a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch as a vehicle's car key. GM said supported vehicles will automatically unlock as you approach and lock when you walk away. You can also open the vehicle's trunk and turn the climate control system on or off right from the Apple Wallet app.


GM's digital keys use ultra-wideband technology to enable secure, proximity-based authentication, along with Bluetooth. They work with the iPhone 11 or later (excluding iPhone SE 2, iPhone SE 3, and iPhone 16e) or an Apple Watch Series 6 or later.

To set up a digital car key, GM said to first download and sign in to your vehicle's mobile app. Then, while in your OnStar-connected GM vehicle with its physical key fob nearby, follow the prompts on the app to add a digital key to your compatible digital wallet of choice. More details are available in Apple's support document.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] El Niño winter forecast: See a map that shows which U.S. regions will get the most snow and rain
items.content_html:
This year’s Super El Niño “looms large” over the winter forecast for the United States, forecasters from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) wrote this week.

And for about half of the country, that’s shaping up to make for a wet winter. 

El Niño is a climate phenomenon defined by above-average sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, and a weakening of trade winds that flow from east to west. All those changes affect atmospheric conditions, disrupting global weather patterns.

How will the phenomenon impact U.S. weather patterns?

El Niños typically present with wetter conditions across the U.S. South, and drier than conditions farther north.

A 2026-2027 Winter Outlook map from NOAA illustrates that, showing a wavy band cutting across the U.S. that will bring “above normal” precipitation to the southern half of the country. That band swings up to cover the entire California coast and the East Coast, as well.  

Certain areas will be impacted even more: parts of Florida, for example, are forecasted to experience 70-80% above normal precipitation.

“As we know from decades of observations, a very strong El Niño will likely bring a southward and eastward shift to the jet stream for the contiguous U.S., which tilts the odds toward stormier weather across the South,” Ken Graham, director of NOAA’s National Weather Service (NWS), said in a statement. 

That wet weather could ease drought conditions in the southwest. Southern Great Plains, Southeast, and parts of the East Coast, according to another NOAA map. 

But forecasters say that could make for other negative weather impacts.

“While higher chances of rain and snow may bring relief to drought-afflicted areas, too much precipitation on dry soil can fuel destructive flash floods and mudslides,” Graham said. “Now is the time for communities and individuals to plan ahead for the upcoming winter.” 

Some communities are already preparing. Governor Gavin Newsom of California has already declared a state of emergency ahead of this El Niño winter. 

With this El Niño already breaking records and potentially only getting stronger, “that can mean repeated rounds of heavy rain, strong winds, mountain snow, flooding, landslides, debris flows, large waves, and coastal flooding, especially when storms hit during very high tides” for California, according to his office. 

Certain areas of the country are expected to see drier-than-average conditions, though, like Hawaii, Alaska, the northern Mountain West, and some areas around the Great Lakes.

That also means drought conditions could “develop or worsen,” forecasters wrote, across some of the northern Rockies, as well as northeastern Oregon and eastern Washington.

Those forecasts mirror others looking ahead to this winter, including a series of maps from AccuWeather that was shared with Fast Company earlier this month.

Word to the wise: The map is not the territory

Experts do note that specific outcomes aren’t a guarantee; the El Niño simply tilts the odds toward certain impacts. As the season gets closer, meteorologists will continue to update their forecasts. 

For those who want to keep a close eye on any oncoming snow or rain, the NWS has now opened its Probabilistic Precipitation Portal, an interactive map that lets users see “the low-end, expected, and high-end amounts of snow, ice and rain” over a 72-hour period.
